quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The doctor examined [I] carefully and said everything was fine.
quests.hint: We need an object pronoun here, since this word comes after the verb 'examined.'
quests.explanation: Object pronouns like 'me' follow verbs, so 'examined me' is correct, not the subject pronoun 'I.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My sister felt sick, so I took [she] to see a doctor right away.
quests.hint: We need an object pronoun here, since it comes after the verb 'took.'
quests.explanation: 'Her' is the object pronoun that follows the verb 'took,' not the subject pronoun 'she.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The nurse gave [we] some medicine for the pain in the morning.
quests.hint: We need a plural object pronoun after the verb 'gave.'
quests.explanation: 'Us' is the object pronoun matching 'we' and follows the verb 'gave,' not the subject pronoun 'we.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The singer thanked [we] warmly for coming to the concert.
quests.hint: We need an object pronoun after the verb 'thanked.'
quests.explanation: 'Us' is the object pronoun form of 'we,' used after the verb 'thanked,' not the subject pronoun 'we.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I really like this band; their new song makes [I] want to dance.
quests.hint: We need an object pronoun after the verb 'makes.'
quests.explanation: 'Me' is the object pronoun that follows the verb 'makes,' not the subject pronoun 'I.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The movie was so funny that it made [they] laugh the whole time.
quests.hint: We need a plural object pronoun after the verb 'made.'
quests.explanation: 'Them' is the object pronoun matching 'they,' used after the verb 'made,' not the subject pronoun 'they.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [check always] my email before I leave for work in the morning.
quests.hint: Frequency adverbs like 'always' usually go before the main verb, not after it.
quests.explanation: Frequency adverbs such as 'always' are placed before the main verb: 'always check,' not 'check always.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [answers never] messages late at night because she goes to bed early.
quests.hint: Frequency adverbs like 'never' usually go before the main verb, not after it.
quests.explanation: 'Never' is placed before the main verb: 'never answers,' not 'answers never.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [call usually] our grandparents on Sunday afternoons every week.
quests.hint: Frequency adverbs like 'usually' usually go before the main verb, not after it.
quests.explanation: 'Usually' is placed before the main verb: 'usually call,' not 'call usually.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [make always] my bed as soon as I wake up each day.
quests.hint: This frequency word belongs right before the verb it describes.
quests.explanation: 'Always' is placed before the main verb: 'always make,' not 'make always.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: He [skips rarely] breakfast, maybe once or twice a year at most.
quests.hint: Frequency adverbs like 'rarely' usually go before the main verb, not after it.
quests.explanation: 'Rarely' is placed before the main verb: 'rarely skips,' not 'skips rarely.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [go always] for a walk after dinner; it's part of our routine.
quests.hint: Check that the frequency adverb sits ahead of the verb, not trailing after it.
quests.explanation: 'Always' is placed before the main verb: 'always go,' not 'go always.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: This year's exam was [more harder] than last year's exam.
quests.hint: Short adjectives form comparatives with -er alone, not with both -er and 'more.'
quests.explanation: Short adjectives like 'hard' use only the -er ending: 'harder,' never both 'more' and '-er' together.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My new classroom is [brighter than than] my old one.
quests.hint: The word 'than' should only appear once in a comparative sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Than' should appear only once after a comparative adjective: 'brighter than,' not repeated twice.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: History class is [more interestinger] than mathematics class, in my opinion.
quests.hint: Longer adjectives use 'more' instead of an -er ending, and never combine both.
quests.explanation: Longer adjectives like 'interesting' use 'more' alone: 'more interesting,' never adding -er as well.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: This job is [more easier] than my last one because I work from home.
quests.hint: Adjectives ending in -y change to -ier in the comparative, without adding 'more' as well.
quests.explanation: 'Easy' becomes 'easier' in the comparative; adding 'more' as well, as in 'more easier,' is incorrect.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Our new office is [more modern than than] the old building downtown.
quests.hint: Check that 'than' isn't accidentally repeated in this comparison.
quests.explanation: 'Than' should appear only once after a comparative phrase: 'more modern than,' not repeated.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My new manager is [more friendlier] than the previous one.
quests.hint: Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y typically change to -ier alone, without adding 'more.'
quests.explanation: 'Friendly' becomes 'friendlier' in the comparative; adding 'more' as well is incorrect and redundant.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We don't have [many time] before our flight departs, so let's hurry to the gate.
quests.hint: 'Time' is an uncountable noun - which quantity word matches it?
quests.explanation: 'Time' is uncountable, so it pairs with 'much,' not 'many,' which is reserved for countable plural nouns.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: There aren't [much seats] left on this train, so we should hurry.
quests.hint: 'Seats' is a countable plural noun - which quantity word matches it?
quests.explanation: 'Seats' is countable and plural, so it pairs with 'many,' not 'much,' which is for uncountable nouns.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We met [much interesting travelers] at the hostel last night.
quests.hint: 'Travelers' is a countable plural noun - which quantity word matches it?
quests.explanation: 'Travelers' is countable and plural, so 'many' is correct, not 'much,' which is used with uncountable nouns.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Do you have [much photos] from your cousin's wedding last month?
quests.hint: 'Photos' is a countable plural noun - which quantity word matches it?
quests.explanation: 'Photos' is countable and plural, so 'many' is correct, not 'much,' which pairs with uncountable nouns.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My uncle has [many advice] about starting a small business.
quests.hint: 'Advice' is an uncountable noun - which quantity word matches it?
quests.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable, so it pairs with 'much,' not 'many,' which is reserved for countable nouns.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: There isn't [many reason] to worry; everyone in the family is doing fine.
quests.hint: 'Reason' here is singular and uncountable in this context - which quantity word fits?
quests.explanation: Used this way, 'reason' pairs with 'much,' not 'many,' which is reserved for countable plural nouns.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The big winter sale always starts [on December], right before the holidays.
quests.hint: Think about the preposition we use with months.
quests.explanation: 'In' is used with months, such as 'in December,' not 'on December.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The shop closes early [in Sundays] for the rest of the year.
quests.hint: Think about the preposition we use with days of the week.
quests.explanation: 'On' is used with specific days, such as 'on Sundays,' not 'in Sundays.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Most online orders arrive [on five business days] from the order date.
quests.hint: Think about a preposition meaning 'before this period of time ends.'
quests.explanation: 'Within' expresses a time limit before a period ends, such as 'within five days,' not 'on five days.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We always eat a big family dinner [in New Year's Eve] every single year.
quests.hint: Think about the preposition used with specific calendar dates or named days.
quests.explanation: 'On' is used with specific days or dates, such as 'on New Year's Eve,' not 'in New Year's Eve.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The restaurant serves a special menu [at the holiday season] every year.
quests.hint: Think about the preposition meaning 'throughout a period of time.'
quests.explanation: 'During' describes something happening throughout a period, such as a season, not 'at.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Breakfast is served [on seven o'clock] every single morning at the hotel.
quests.hint: Think about the preposition we use with exact clock times.
quests.explanation: 'At' is used with precise times, such as 'at seven o'clock,' not 'on seven o'clock.'
